declared.title: The mnemonic effect of central and peripheral misinformation on social media
declared.foundIn: reports/memory-rewritten/counter-evidence.md (card 6); Crossref search « susceptibility peripheral central false information tweets memory culture », from 2023 (2026-11-26)

population: 425 European American and Asian or Asian American college students (US), in a simulated online setting: GIFs of daily-life events, then tweets

findings.text: In both studies and both cultural groups, people falsely recognized more of the false details they had read in tweets than false details they had not read

support.sentence: Regardless of cultural background, participants in both studies demonstrated the misinformation effect, whereby they falsely recognised more and resisted less tweeted than untweeted false information.

findings.text: People were more easily misled about peripheral details of an event than about its central details

support.sentence: Furthermore, they showed higher susceptibility to peripheral than central false information exposed via tweets.

limits: daily-life clips and tweets from strangers, a true/false test: not a talk with a colleague, not one's own life
in Study 2, Asian participants were less influenced than European Americans (abstract): no sign of a larger effect in « collectivist » groups
US college students; no sample from the Middle East or North Africa
the abstract gives no rates: how much less for central details is in the full text (closed, not read)
